title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark
explain_beginner: This 2021 paper by Raji and colleagues asks whether a few popular AI tests really show how close we are to building broadly capable AI. The authors say people often treat strong scores on these tests as proof of general progress. But the tests cover only selected problems, so they may not measure the wider abilities they are supposed to represent. The paper argues a viewpoint rather than presenting new experiments. It warns that using narrow benchmarks as general measures can mislead. That matters because such scores shape how progress is understood and judged.
explain_business: This paper warns executives not to treat a strong score on a popular AI benchmark as proof that a system is broadly capable. Raji and colleagues argue that such scores often reflect narrow tasks, while being presented as signs of general progress. In practice, leaders should ask what a benchmark actually measures, what it leaves out, and whether it matches the broad claims made about it. The decision it informs is how much weight to give benchmark results when judging AI progress or capability. Use them as one signal, not as a final verdict.
explain_practitioner: Raji and colleagues present a 2021 paper that argues a viewpoint. They examine how AI subfields elevate a few widely used benchmarks and treat top scores as evidence of movement toward broad, adaptable intelligence. They explore the limits of these benchmarks by asking what they actually measure and whether that supports the general claims made about them. The key result is that this framing has validity problems. A benchmark can be useful for a narrow task while failing to justify broad conclusions about general AI progress. The authors therefore challenge the practice of using such scores as overall measures.
